title: Frequency Domain: Fourier Series
notes:
Activity "Frequency Domain: Fourier Series" (PHY/EGR 3120), on the fourier Tool. Part 1 builds the square and triangle waves from their series (Synthesis Mode); Parts 2 and 3 take a sine and the square wave apart by hand (Analysis Mode). Part 4 passes the square wave through the RC low-pass (Synthesis Mode, where the time plot shows the filtered sum and its N = ∞ curve): gain only, phase only, both, then one harmonic by hand; a Task then unlocks the filter type for the switch to high-pass, its spikes, its 3rd harmonic and the two gains' sum.

Prompts and Questions may use \( \) math; the ones students answer use Unicode subscripts so they read the same either way.

Conditions, numeric and choice keys, and Hints that would give an answer away are encoded answer keys (framework/v1/authoring/encode-keys.html, or encodeKey() from framework/v1/runner/keys.js); decode one with decodeKey(). The keys agree with the engine (tests/unit/fourier/activity.test.js checks them against series() and productAverage()). Tolerances: amplitudes (and aₙ, bₙ) 2% relative, or 0.01 V absolute for a zero amplitude; phases ±2° judged mod 360°, so −90° and 270° both pass. The N Conditions accept a band about the smallest N within 5% (from a little below it, where the error is just over 5%), since students judge it by eye. Hints guide and never state the passing value. Points: 1 per Task with a Condition, none for a Task without one, 1 per graded Question. A zero amplitude takes the absolute tolerance because a relative one would leave none.

Every Setup fixes f₀ = 1 kHz, ±1 V and no offset.

parts.title: Part 1: Square vs Triangle
parts.notes: The Setup fixes the filter off, and the first Task locks the signal and filter Controls (amp, f0, offset, shift, filter, fc, applyGain, applyPhase).

tasks.title: How fast the terms fall
tasks.prompt: The sidebar's coefficient table lists each harmonic's amplitude Aₙ and phase φₙ for the selected waveform, written as Aₙ cos(nω₀t + φₙ). Switch the waveform between Square and Triangle and compare how fast Aₙ falls as n grows.

questions.prompt: How do the nonzero Aₙ fall with n?

choices.text: Square Aₙ ∝ 1/n; triangle Aₙ ∝ 1/n²
Square Aₙ ∝ 1/n²; triangle Aₙ ∝ 1/n
Both fall as 1/n
Both fall as 1/n²

tasks.title: Building the square wave
tasks.prompt: Select the Square wave. Raise N until the partial sum stays within 5% of the square wave (±0.05 V) everywhere more than 0.1 ms from a jump, and stop at the smallest N that does. Press Play to watch the sum build up, then fine-tune N with the slider.

hint.text: Judge the wiggles on the flat tops, not the overshoot right at each jump: that overshoot never shrinks, however large N gets. Each new odd harmonic squeezes the wiggles closer to the jumps.

tasks.title: Building the triangle wave
tasks.prompt: Now select the Triangle wave and find the smallest N that keeps the sum within 5% (±0.05 V) of the triangle everywhere more than 0.1 ms from a corner.

hint.text: The triangle's sum is furthest off at the corners, which you can ignore here; look between them. Compare the table: the triangle's terms shrink much faster than the square's.

tasks.title: Jumps, corners and two descriptions
tasks.prompt: Answer each in a few sentences.

questions.prompt: Why does a waveform with jumps (the square) need many more terms than one with only corners (the triangle)? Relate your answer to how fast Aₙ falls.
The waveform and its table of Aₙ and φₙ describe the same signal two ways. What does each description make easy to see?

parts.title: Part 2: A Sine
parts.notes: The Setup fixes the filter off, and the first Task locks the signal and filter Controls and the waveform (amp, f0, offset, shift, filter, fc, applyGain, applyPhase, waveform). It hides the spectrum and the filter curves; the Task after the coefficient Tasks shows the spectrum, and the filter curves stay hidden.

tasks.title: a₁ and b₁ by hand
tasks.prompt: The input is a 1 V, 1 kHz sine, v(t) = sin(ω₀t). The product plot shows the input times the test function over one period T, with positive and negative area shaded. The net area gives \(a_n = \frac{2}{T}\int_0^T v(t)\cos(n\omega_0 t)\,dt\) with the cos test function, and \(b_n = \frac{2}{T}\int_0^T v(t)\sin(n\omega_0 t)\,dt\) with sin. Compute a₁ and b₁ by hand.

hint.text: Look at where the shaded areas of each product lie over the period, and which ones cancel. By hand: over one period, sin² averages to one half and cos·sin averages to zero.

tasks.title: A₁ and φ₁
tasks.prompt: Write the harmonic in cos form, A₁ cos(ω₀t + φ₁), where \(a_1 = A_1\cos\varphi_1\) and \(b_1 = -A_1\sin\varphi_1\). Give φ₁ in degrees.

hint.text: A₁ = √(a₁² + b₁²). For φ₁, cos φ₁ has the sign of a₁ and sin φ₁ the sign of −b₁. With a₁ zero an arctangent is no help: find the angle whose cosine is zero and whose sine has the sign of −b₁.

tasks.title: Other harmonics
tasks.prompt: The spectrum is now shown: check your A₁ and φ₁ against it. Then set n to 2 and to 3, with each test function, and look at the shaded areas.

questions.prompt: What do the n = 2 and n = 3 products show?

choices.text: Their positive and negative areas cancel, so a₂, b₂, a₃ and b₃ are all zero: the sine has no 2nd or 3rd harmonic.
Their net areas are small but not zero, so the sine has weak 2nd and 3rd harmonics.
Only the cos products cancel; the sin products leave a net area.
They cancel only because this sine starts at zero at t = 0.

parts.title: Part 3: The Square Wave
parts.notes: The Setup fixes the filter off, and the first Task locks the signal and filter Controls and the waveform (amp, f0, offset, shift, filter, fc, applyGain, applyPhase, waveform). It hides the spectrum and the filter curves; the Task after the coefficient Tasks shows the spectrum, and the filter curves stay hidden.

tasks.title: Aₙ and φₙ for n = 1 to 5
tasks.prompt: The input is the 1 V, 1 kHz square wave: +1 V for the first half period and −1 V for the second. Use the product plot to compute aₙ and bₙ by hand for n = 1 to 5, then give each Aₙ, and φₙ for the odd n. Enter 0 for an amplitude that is zero. Why φₙ is −90°: this square wave is an odd function of t, like sin, so every cos product cancels and aₙ = 0. Each nonzero harmonic is then a positive multiple of sin(nω₀t), and sin x = cos(x − 90°), so written in the cos form Aₙ cos(nω₀t + φₙ) its phase is φₙ = −90°. We use the cos form because the phasor Activity next builds on it.

hint.text: Split the integral for bₙ at the half period: the wave is a constant on each half, so each piece is the integral of sin(nω₀t) over half a period. For even n the two halves cancel; for odd n they add.

tasks.title: The pattern
tasks.prompt: The spectrum is now shown: check your Aₙ and φₙ against it.

questions.prompt: What pattern do the square wave's coefficients follow?

choices.text: The even terms are zero, and Aₙ ∝ 1/n for odd n.
The even terms are zero, and Aₙ ∝ 1/n² for odd n.
Every term is nonzero, and Aₙ ∝ 1/n.
The odd terms are zero, and Aₙ ∝ 1/n for even n.

parts.title: Part 4: RC Filters on the Square Wave
parts.notes: The Setup fixes the square wave, f_c = 3 kHz and the low-pass with both toggles off. The first Task locks all but the toggles (waveform, amp, f0, offset, shift, filter, fc) and unlocks the toggles (applyGain, applyPhase), whose states the toggle Tasks' Conditions check. The switch Task unlocks the filter type (its Condition checks high-pass with both toggles on), and the Task after it locks the filter type again.

tasks.title: Low-pass: gain only
tasks.prompt: The 1 V, 1 kHz square wave now feeds the first-order RC low-pass filter from the RC Activity, with f_c = 3 kHz. The filter acts on each harmonic in two ways: Apply gain scales its amplitude by the gain |H| at its frequency, and Apply phase shift adds the phase shift ∠H to its phase. Turn on Apply gain only, and compare the partial sum and the N = ∞ curve with the square wave.

tasks.title: Low-pass: phase only
tasks.prompt: Now turn on Apply phase shift only: every harmonic keeps its amplitude but is delayed by the filter. Compare the shape with the square wave and with the gain-only shape.

tasks.title: Low-pass: gain and phase
tasks.prompt: Turn on both Apply gain and Apply phase shift. Try each of the three settings again if you like, and raise N to watch the partial sum approach the N = ∞ curve.

questions.prompt: Which setting turns the square wave into the RC charging curve, V_C rising and falling exponentially toward ±1 V?

choices.text: Gain only
Phase only
Gain and phase together
Either one alone

questions.prompt: Why does the filter need both its gain and its phase shift to produce the RC charging curve? What goes wrong with each one alone?

tasks.title: Low-pass: the output 3rd harmonic
tasks.prompt: Hand-compute the filtered output's 3rd harmonic, from the input's A₃ and φ₃ (Part 3). The first-order RC low-pass filter has gain |H| = 1/√(1 + (f/f_c)²) and phase shift ∠H = −arctan(f/f_c), at the harmonic's frequency f. The output harmonic has amplitude A₃·|H| and phase φ₃ + ∠H.

hint.text: The 3rd harmonic is at f = 3f₀: start from f/f_c there. Multiply the input's A₃ by |H|, and add ∠H, in degrees, to the input's φ₃.

tasks.title: Switch to high-pass
tasks.prompt: The Filter type is now unlocked. Switch it to High-pass: the output is now the voltage V_R across the resistor, with the same f_c = 3 kHz. Try gain only and phase only on the high-pass if you like, then submit with both Apply gain and Apply phase shift on.

questions.prompt: Which setting turns the square wave into the decaying spikes you measured, V_R jumping by 2 V at each edge and then decaying exponentially toward 0?

choices.text: Gain only
Phase only
Gain and phase together
Either one alone

tasks.title: High-pass: the output 3rd harmonic
tasks.prompt: Hand-compute the high-pass output's 3rd harmonic, from the input's A₃ and φ₃ (Part 3). The first-order RC high-pass filter has gain |H| = 1/√(1 + (f_c/f)²) and phase shift ∠H = arctan(f_c/f), at the harmonic's frequency f. The output harmonic has amplitude A₃·|H| and phase φ₃ + ∠H.

hint.text: The 3rd harmonic is at f = 3f₀: start from f_c/f there. Multiply the input's A₃ by |H|, and add ∠H, in degrees, to the input's φ₃. The high-pass ∠H is positive: it shifts the phase forward rather than back.

tasks.title: Do the gains add to 1?
tasks.prompt: Low-pass gives V_C and high-pass gives V_R, and V_C + V_R = v_in. The low-pass gain is H_LP = 1/(1 + j f/f_c) and the high-pass gain is H_HP = (j f/f_c)/(1 + j f/f_c). Compare the two at f = 3 kHz.

questions.prompt: Which statement explains why V_C + V_R = v_in?

choices.text: The complex gains add to 1 at every f, H_LP + H_HP = 1, though their magnitudes do not: the phase shifts matter.
The magnitudes add to 1 at every f, |H_LP| + |H_HP| = 1, so the amplitudes split between V_C and V_R.
The gains add to 1 only at f = 0, so V_C + V_R = v_in only for the DC term.
Neither adds to 1: V_C + V_R = v_in only at N = ∞.
